phy_ocra.6.0.summary: Electric charge is a property of all matter: protons carry positive charge, electrons carry negative charge, and objects are normally neutral because these balance. When two insulating materials are rubbed together, friction transfers **electrons** from one surface to the other, leaving one negatively charged (gained electrons) and the other positively charged (lost electrons). Like charges repel and unlike charges attract, even without contact, and if enough charge builds up it can jump through the air as a **spark**.

core.h: Charge is a property of all matter
core.p: All matter is made of atoms, and atoms contain charged particles. The **protons** in the nucleus are positive and the **electrons** around the nucleus are negative. Neutrons have no charge.
bullets: Two types of charge: **positive** and **negative**
Proton charge: +1 (relative); electron charge: -1 (relative)
An atom has equal numbers of protons and electrons, so it is **neutral** overall
A neutral object still contains huge amounts of charge; the positive and negative simply balance
Charge is measured in **coulombs (C)**

callouts.p: Neutral does not mean no charge. It means equal amounts of positive and negative charge.

core.p: Charged objects exert forces on each other **without touching**. The force acts through the electric field around each charge.
bullets: **Like charges repel**: positive and positive, negative and negative
**Unlike (opposite) charges attract**: positive and negative
The force is a **non-contact force**
The force is stronger when charges are closer together
The force is stronger when the charges are bigger

callouts.p: Like charges repel; unlike charges attract.

core.p: When two different **insulating** materials are rubbed together, **friction** makes electrons move from one surface to the other. Because insulators do not let charge flow, the charge stays where it is: it is **static**.
bullets: Only **electrons** are transferred; protons stay locked in the nuclei
The material that **gains electrons** becomes **negatively charged**
The material that **loses electrons** becomes **positively charged**
The two objects end up with **equal and opposite** charges
Examples: polythene rod rubbed with a cloth becomes negative; acetate (or perspex) rod rubbed with a cloth becomes positive
Rubbing a balloon on hair or a jumper charges the balloon

callouts.p: Never say positive charges or protons move. An object becomes positive by losing electrons.

core.p: The whole of static electricity is explained by electrons moving. Use this chain in every explanation: rubbing, friction, electrons move from A to B, B gains electrons so is negative, A loses electrons so is positive.
bullets: Polythene and cloth: electrons move **from the cloth to the polythene**
Polythene gains electrons: negative; cloth loses electrons: positive
Acetate and cloth: electrons move **from the acetate to the cloth**
Acetate loses electrons: positive; cloth gains electrons: negative
Charge is **conserved**: no charge is created or destroyed, it is only moved

callouts.p: Write: electrons are transferred from the cloth to the rod, so the rod gains electrons and becomes negatively charged.

core.p: In a **conductor** such as a metal, electrons move freely. Any charge given to it flows away through your hand to Earth. In an **insulator**, electrons cannot move freely, so charge stays on the surface where it was transferred.
bullets: Insulators: plastic, rubber, glass, dry wool, polythene, acetate
Conductors: metals, the human body (weakly), damp air
A metal rod held in an insulating handle can be charged
Earthing: connecting to the ground lets electrons flow and removes static charge

callouts.p: Connecting a charged object to the ground with a conductor so that electrons flow to or from the Earth, removing the charge.

core.h: Evidence for forces between charged objects
core.p: Simple experiments show that charged objects attract or repel each other without contact.
bullets: Hang a charged polythene rod so it can turn freely; bring a second charged polythene rod near: it **turns away** (repulsion)
Bring a charged acetate rod near the hanging polythene rod: it **turns towards** it (attraction)
Two charged balloons hung side by side push apart
Charged hair strands stand up and move apart because they have like charges
A charged rod can deflect a thin stream of water from a tap

callouts.p: Repulsion is the only sure test that an object is charged, because a charged object can also attract a neutral object.

core.p: A charged object can attract small neutral objects such as bits of paper, or stick a balloon to a wall. The charged object pushes or pulls electrons in the neutral object, so the near side gets an opposite charge (this is called **induction**).
bullets: Negative balloon near a wall repels electrons in the wall surface away
The wall surface near the balloon becomes slightly positive
Unlike charges are closer than like charges, so attraction wins
The balloon sticks to the wall

core.p: If a lot of charge builds up, the potential difference between the object and nearby objects (or Earth) becomes very large. Eventually electrons jump across the air gap, making a **spark**.
bullets: Large build-up of charge gives a large potential difference
Air is normally an insulator, but a very high potential difference makes it conduct
Electrons flow through the air: a **spark** and a crackle
Getting a shock from a car door or metal handle after walking on a nylon carpet
Lightning is a giant spark from charged clouds

callouts.p: A spark happens when charge has built up, not simply because two objects touch.

core.p: Sparks are dangerous near flammable gases or fine powders, and electronic components can be damaged by static discharges.
bullets: Refuelling aircraft and fuel tankers: fuel flowing through pipes can build up charge; a spark could ignite fuel vapour
Prevented by **earthing** the tanker or plane with a conducting cable
Grain silos and flour mills: dust explosions
Operating theatres and electronics factories use anti-static floors and wrist straps

core.p: Static electricity is useful whenever charged particles need to be attracted to a surface.
bullets: Paint spraying: charged paint droplets repel each other into a fine spray and are attracted to an oppositely charged object, giving an even coat
Photocopiers and laser printers use charged drums to pick up toner
Electrostatic precipitators remove smoke particles from chimneys
Dust attraction to TV screens and dusters

callouts.p: Mention both: droplets repel each other (fine spray) and are attracted to the object (less waste, reaches hidden parts).

core.p: Six-mark questions on static usually combine charging, forces and sparks. Use precise words throughout.
bullets: Name the particles: **electrons** transferred by **friction**
State which way electrons move and the resulting charge on each object
Use **like charges repel / unlike charges attract** to explain movement
Use **build-up of charge** and **electrons jump** to explain sparks
Suggest earthing as the way to stop charge building up

analogy.p: Imagine every object starts with equal numbers of red stickers (protons, glued down) and blue stickers (electrons, loosely stuck). Rubbing two objects together is like brushing past someone: some blue stickers rub off one and onto the other. The one with extra blue stickers is negative; the one missing blue stickers is positive. Red stickers never move. The analogy breaks down because stickers do not push or pull on each other at a distance, whereas charges attract and repel without touching.

terms.d: A property of matter that causes it to experience a force in an electric field; positive or negative.
A negatively charged particle outside the nucleus; the only particle transferred when objects are charged by friction.
A positively charged particle in the nucleus.
Having equal amounts of positive and negative charge, so no overall charge.
Charge that builds up on the surface of an insulator and stays there.
A material in which electrons cannot move freely, so charge cannot flow through it.
A material in which electrons can move freely, allowing charge to flow.
A force between surfaces rubbing together; in static electricity it causes electrons to be transferred.
A force pushing two objects apart; occurs between like charges.
A force pulling two objects together; occurs between unlike charges.
A force that acts between objects that are not touching, such as the electrostatic force.
A flow of electrons through air when a large charge builds up and the potential difference is high enough.
Connecting an object to the ground with a conductor so excess charge can flow away.
The unit of electric charge.
Charge cannot be created or destroyed, only transferred.

mistakes.w: The rod becomes positive because it gains protons.
mistakes.r: The rod becomes positive because it loses electrons; protons do not move.

mistakes.w: Positive charges move from the cloth to the rod.
mistakes.r: Only electrons (negative charges) are transferred.

mistakes.w: Rubbing creates charge.
mistakes.r: Rubbing transfers electrons; charge is conserved, not created.

mistakes.w: Like charges attract.
mistakes.r: Like charges repel; unlike charges attract.

mistakes.w: Attraction proves an object is charged.
mistakes.r: A charged object can attract a neutral one; only repulsion proves both are charged.

mistakes.w: Metals cannot be charged at all.
mistakes.r: A metal held in your hand loses charge to Earth; held by an insulating handle, it can be charged.

mistakes.w: A spark is caused by friction heating the air.
mistakes.r: A spark is caused by a large build-up of charge, so electrons jump across the air gap.

mistakes.w: Neutral objects have no charges in them.
mistakes.r: Neutral objects contain equal amounts of positive and negative charge.

exam.q: State the charge on an electron.
model: Negative (relative charge -1)
exam.tip: One word is enough: negative.

exam.q: Two negatively charged balloons are hung close together. Describe what happens and why.
model: They move apart
Because like charges repel
exam.tip: Describe then explain.

exam.q: A polythene rod is rubbed with a cloth and becomes negatively charged. Explain how this happens.
model: Friction between the rod and cloth
Transfers electrons from the cloth to the rod
The rod gains electrons so has more negative than positive charge
exam.tip: Name electrons and give the direction.

exam.q: State the charge on the cloth in the previous question and explain your answer.
model: Positive
It has lost electrons (so has more protons than electrons)
exam.tip: Equal and opposite charge.

exam.q: Explain why only electrons, and not protons, are transferred when objects are rubbed.
model: Protons are held in the nucleus
Electrons are outside the nucleus and can be removed / are free to move
exam.tip: Location of the particles is the key idea.

exam.q: Explain why an insulator can be charged by rubbing but a metal rod held in the hand cannot.
model: In an insulator electrons cannot move freely, so charge stays on the surface
In a metal, electrons move freely
Charge flows through the metal and the person to Earth
exam.tip: Compare both materials.

exam.q: A charged acetate rod is brought near a suspended charged polythene rod. Describe and explain what is seen.
model: The polythene rod moves / turns towards the acetate rod
Acetate is positive and polythene is negative
Unlike charges attract
exam.tip: Give the charges on both rods.

exam.q: A person walks across a nylon carpet and gets a shock when touching a metal door handle. Explain why.
model: Friction between shoes and carpet transfers electrons
Charge builds up on the person
When near the metal handle, the potential difference is large enough for electrons to jump
Electrons flow to/from the handle (to Earth), causing a spark / shock
exam.tip: Charging, build-up, then discharge.

exam.q: Explain why a fuel tanker is connected to the ground with a cable before unloading.
model: Fuel flowing / friction can cause charge to build up on the tanker
A spark could ignite the fuel vapour and cause an explosion
The cable earths the tanker so charge flows away safely
exam.tip: Hazard, then how earthing prevents it.

exam.q: Describe how static charge is produced when a balloon is rubbed on a jumper, and explain how the charged balloon can stick to a neutral wall and can repel another charged balloon.
model: Friction transfers electrons from the jumper to the balloon
The balloon gains electrons and becomes negative; the jumper becomes positive
The negative balloon repels electrons in the wall surface away from it
The wall surface nearest the balloon becomes positive
Unlike charges attract, so the balloon sticks to the wall
A second negatively charged balloon is repelled because like charges repel
exam.tip: Cover charging, induction and repulsion in order.

worked.q: An acetate rod is rubbed with a cloth and becomes positively charged. Model answer: explain how the rod and cloth become charged.
steps: Friction between the rod and the cloth transfers electrons
Electrons move from the acetate rod to the cloth
The rod has lost electrons so it has more protons than electrons: positive
The cloth has gained electrons: negative
The charges are equal in size and opposite in sign, because charge is conserved
worked.ans: The rod is positive and the cloth is negative because electrons are transferred from the rod to the cloth.

worked.q: Applied example: explain how electrostatic paint spraying gives an even coat with little waste.
steps: The paint droplets are given the same charge as they leave the spray gun
Like charges repel, so the droplets spread out into a fine, even spray
The object to be painted is given the opposite charge (or earthed)
Unlike charges attract, so droplets are pulled onto the object, even onto hidden surfaces
Fewer droplets miss the object, so less paint is wasted
worked.ans: Repulsion between droplets gives a fine spray; attraction to the object gives an even coat and little waste.

phy_ocra.6.1.summary: Every charged object is surrounded by an **electric field**: a region in which another charge feels a **non-contact force**. The field is strongest close to the charged object and gets weaker with distance, and we draw it with **field lines** that show the direction of the force on a small positive charge. Electric fields explain why charged objects attract or repel without touching, and why sparks jump when the field becomes strong enough to ionise the air.

core.p: A charged object creates an **electric field** in the space around it. Any other charged object placed in that field experiences a **force**. Because the force acts through the field, the two objects do not need to touch: the electrostatic force is a **non-contact force**.
bullets: The field exists whether or not a second charge is there to feel it.
Only **charged** objects feel a force from an electric field; neutral objects are not pushed directly.
The force on the second object is caused by the field of the first, and the first feels an equal and opposite force from the field of the second.
Electric fields belong in the same family as gravitational and magnetic fields: all are regions where a non-contact force acts.

callouts.p: A region around a charged object in which another charged object experiences a force.

core.p: The electric field is **strongest close to the charged object** and becomes **weaker further away**. So the force on a second charge is larger when it is nearer, and smaller when it is further away.
bullets: Move a charge closer: the force on it increases.
Move a charge further away: the force on it decreases.
A larger charge on the object gives a stronger field at the same distance.
A larger charge placed in the field feels a bigger force.

callouts.p: The closer you are to a charged object, the stronger its electric field and the bigger the force on another charge.

core.p: We show an electric field with **field lines**. The arrow on each line shows the **direction of the force on a small positive charge** placed at that point.
bullets: Field lines point **away from positive** charges and **towards negative** charges.
Field lines never cross each other.
Where lines are **closer together** the field is **stronger**.
Field lines meet the surface of a conductor at **right angles** (90 degrees).
A negative charge placed in the field feels a force in the **opposite** direction to the arrows.

callouts.p: Always put arrows on field lines. A diagram without arrows usually loses the direction mark.

core.h: Field around an isolated charged sphere
core.p: An isolated charged sphere has a **radial** field: the lines spread out in straight lines from the centre, like the spokes of a wheel. For a positive sphere they point outwards; for a negative sphere they point inwards.
bullets: Lines are drawn as if they come from the centre of the sphere.
Lines start at the surface at right angles to it.
The lines spread apart with distance, showing the field getting weaker.
Draw lines evenly spaced around the sphere, with at least 8 lines.

callouts.p: Do not draw curved or uneven lines for a single sphere. The pattern must be straight, radial and evenly spaced.

core.p: Between two oppositely charged parallel plates the field is **uniform**: it has the same strength and direction everywhere between the plates (except near the edges).
bullets: Lines are **straight, parallel and equally spaced**.
Lines go from the **positive plate to the negative plate**.
Equal spacing shows the field strength is the same everywhere in the middle.
Near the edges of the plates the lines bulge outwards and the field is no longer uniform.
A charge anywhere in the uniform region feels the same size force in the same direction.

callouts.p: A field with the same strength and direction at every point.

core.p: The field line direction tells you the force on a positive charge. A **positive charge** is pushed **along** the field lines; a **negative charge** such as an electron is pushed **against** them.
bullets: In a field pointing right, a proton is pushed right and an electron is pushed left.
Between plates, electrons are pulled towards the positive plate.
This explains attraction of opposite charges and repulsion of like charges.
The force on a charge is the same as the force it would feel from all the charges making the field.

core.h: Explaining attraction and repulsion with fields
core.p: When two charged objects are near each other, each one sits in the field of the other. The **field of one object exerts a force on the charge of the other**. Like charges are pushed apart; unlike charges are pulled together.
bullets: Two positive rods: each is in the outward field of the other, so each is pushed away.
Positive and negative: the negative charge is pushed against the field lines, towards the positive object.
The forces are equal in size and opposite in direction.
The forces get bigger as the objects get closer because the fields are stronger there.

callouts.p: In explanation questions say: the charged object creates an electric field; the other charge is in this field; so it experiences a force.

core.p: If a charged object builds up a large charge, the electric field near it becomes very strong. A strong enough field can pull electrons off air particles (**ionising** the air). The air becomes a conductor and charge flows through it as a **spark**.
bullets: Sparks jump more easily when the gap is small, because the field is stronger close to the charge.
Large charge plus small distance gives the strongest field.
Pointed parts of a conductor have the strongest field, so sparks jump from points.
Lightning is a huge spark from a charged cloud when the field becomes strong enough to ionise the air.

callouts.p: A spark happens when the electric field is strong enough to ionise air, letting charge flow across the gap.

core.h: Dangers and uses linked to fields
core.p: Strong electric fields around charged objects can cause sparks. Sparks can ignite flammable gases or dust, so charge must be kept from building up in places such as fuel tankers and flour mills.
bullets: Fuel tankers are **earthed** with a wire so charge flows away before the field gets strong enough to cause a spark.
Electrostatic paint sprayers use the field around a charged object to pull charged paint droplets onto it.
Electrostatic precipitators use fields to attract charged smoke particles to plates.
Photocopiers and laser printers use fields to attract toner to charged regions.

callouts.p: Earthing does not stop the field existing; it stops charge building up, so the field never becomes strong enough to cause a spark.

core.h: Drawing field diagrams in the exam
core.p: Field diagram questions are marked on shape, spacing and direction. Use a ruler for straight lines and make the pattern symmetrical.
bullets: Sphere: straight radial lines, evenly spaced, touching the surface at 90 degrees, arrows out for positive and in for negative.
Plates: straight, parallel, evenly spaced lines from + to -, with arrows.
Mention that lines closer together mean a stronger field.
Never let lines cross or stop in the middle of empty space.

callouts.p: For a sphere, draw at least 8 lines and extend them in line with the centre of the sphere.

analogy.p: A charged object is like a campfire. The space around the fire is a zone where you feel warmth, just as the space around a charge is a zone where another charge feels a force. Close to the fire the warmth is strong; far away it is weak, just like field strength falling with distance. Where the analogy breaks down: you feel warmth whether or not you are charged, but only charged objects feel an electric force, and warmth never pulls you closer, whereas an electric field can attract or repel depending on the sign of the charge.

terms.d: A region around a charged object where another charged object experiences a force.
A force that acts between objects that are not touching, for example the electrostatic force.
The attractive or repulsive force between charged objects.
A line showing the direction of the force on a small positive charge placed in the field.
How strong the electric field is at a point; shown by how close together the field lines are.
A field whose lines spread out in straight lines from a central point, as around a charged sphere.
A field with the same strength and direction at every point, as between parallel plates.
Two flat conducting plates with opposite charges, producing a uniform field between them.
Charge that has lost electrons; field lines point away from it.
Charge that has gained electrons; field lines point towards it.
Removing electrons from atoms or molecules so they become charged ions.
A flow of charge through air that has been ionised by a very strong electric field.
Connecting a conductor to the ground so charge can flow away and does not build up.
The force pulling unlike charges towards each other.
The force pushing like charges apart.

mistakes.w: Field lines point towards a positive charge.
mistakes.r: Field lines point away from positive charges and towards negative charges.

mistakes.w: The field is the same strength everywhere around a sphere.
mistakes.r: The field around a sphere is strongest near it and gets weaker with distance.

mistakes.w: The field between parallel plates is stronger near the plates.
mistakes.r: The field between parallel plates is uniform: the same strength everywhere except at the edges.

mistakes.w: Field lines show the direction an electron moves.
mistakes.r: Field lines show the direction of the force on a positive charge; an electron is pushed the opposite way.

mistakes.w: The charges must touch for a force to act.
mistakes.r: The electrostatic force is a non-contact force that acts through the electric field.

mistakes.w: Drew field lines that cross or curve around a single sphere.
mistakes.r: Field lines never cross; around an isolated sphere they are straight and radial.

mistakes.w: A spark is caused by electrons jumping because they are attracted.
mistakes.r: A spark happens when the field is strong enough to ionise the air so charge can flow across the gap.

mistakes.w: Field lines closer together means a weaker field.
mistakes.r: Field lines closer together means a stronger field.

exam.q: What is meant by an electric field?
model: A region where a charged object experiences a force.
exam.tip: Include the word charge and the word force.

exam.q: Draw the electric field pattern around an isolated positively charged sphere.
model: Straight radial lines, evenly spaced, meeting the surface at 90 degrees.
Arrows pointing outwards, away from the sphere.
exam.tip: Use a ruler and at least 8 lines.

exam.q: Draw the electric field between two parallel plates, the top one positive and the bottom one negative.
model: Straight, parallel, equally spaced lines between the plates.
Arrows pointing from the positive plate to the negative plate.
exam.tip: Keep the spacing equal to show the field is uniform.

exam.q: State how the strength of the electric field around a charged sphere changes with distance from it.
model: The field gets weaker as the distance increases.
exam.tip: You can refer to field lines spreading out.

exam.q: An electron is placed between two charged parallel plates. State the direction of the force on it.
model: Towards the positive plate (opposite to the field lines).
exam.tip: Electrons are negative, so they go against the arrows.

exam.q: Explain why a charged balloon can repel another charged balloon without touching it.
model: Each balloon creates an electric field around it.
The other balloon is charged and is in this field so experiences a (repulsive) force; it is a non-contact force.
exam.tip: Link field to force on a charge.

exam.q: Compare the electric field around a charged sphere with the field between parallel plates.
model: Sphere field is radial; plate field has parallel lines.
Sphere field gets weaker with distance.
Plate field is uniform, the same strength everywhere.
Sphere lines point out of positive or into negative; plate lines go from positive to negative plate.
exam.tip: Make each point a direct comparison.

exam.q: A charged metal dome produces a spark to a nearby earthed sphere. Explain why a spark is more likely when the sphere is moved closer.
model: The electric field is stronger closer to the dome.
A strong enough field ionises the air so charge can flow as a spark.
exam.tip: Mention ionisation of air.

exam.q: Explain, in terms of electric fields, how a spark can be produced and why this is dangerous when refuelling an aircraft. Describe how the danger is reduced.
model: Fuel flowing through the pipe causes friction and charge builds up on the aircraft or tanker.
The charge creates an electric field around it.
As charge builds up the field becomes stronger.
When the field is strong enough it ionises the air and a spark jumps.
A spark could ignite fuel vapour and cause an explosion.
The tanker and aircraft are earthed or bonded with a conducting wire so charge flows away and the field never becomes strong enough to spark.
exam.tip: Build a clear chain: charge, field, stronger field, ionisation, spark, ignition, earthing.

exam.q: Two small charged spheres attract each other. State what happens to the force between them when they are moved further apart, and explain why.
model: The force decreases.
Each is in a weaker part of the other's field.
exam.tip: Always give the reason in terms of field strength.

worked.q: A positively charged sphere is placed near a small negatively charged bead. Describe and explain the force on the bead.
steps: The sphere creates a radial electric field pointing outwards.
The bead is charged and sits in this field, so it feels a force.
A negative charge is pushed against the field lines, so the force is towards the sphere.
The bead is attracted; the force increases as it moves closer because the field is stronger near the sphere.
worked.ans: The bead is attracted towards the sphere by a non-contact force that grows stronger as it gets closer.

worked.q: Describe the motion of a proton and an electron released in the middle of a uniform field between two plates, with the top plate positive.
steps: The field lines point from the top (positive) plate down to the bottom (negative) plate.
The proton is positive, so it is pushed along the field lines: downwards.
The electron is negative, so it is pushed against the field lines: upwards.
The field is uniform, so each feels the same size force wherever it is between the plates.
worked.ans: The proton accelerates towards the negative plate and the electron towards the positive plate, each with a constant force.

worked.q: Explain why lightning strikes tall pointed objects.
steps: A thundercloud holds a large charge and creates a strong electric field.
The field is strongest where the gap is smallest and around pointed objects.
Near a tall pointed object the field becomes strong enough to ionise the air first.
Ionised air conducts, so charge flows as a huge spark along that path.
worked.ans: Tall pointed objects are where the field is strongest, so the air ionises there first and the lightning follows that path.

phy_ocra.6.2.summary: **Electric current** is the **rate of flow of charge**: how many coulombs of charge pass a point in the circuit each second. In metal wires the charge is carried by **free electrons**, and charge only flows when there is a **closed circuit** and a **source of potential difference** such as a cell. The amount of charge that flows is linked to current and time by **Q = I x t**, so 1 ampere means 1 coulomb of charge passing each second.

core.h: Current is a rate of flow of charge
core.p: An **electric current** is a **flow of electric charge**. The size of the current tells you **how much charge passes a point each second**. A bigger current means more charge passes the point in the same time.
bullets: Current is measured in **amperes (A)**, often shortened to amps.
Charge is measured in **coulombs (C)**.
Time is measured in **seconds (s)**.
1 ampere = 1 coulomb of charge passing a point every second.
Small currents are often given in milliamps: 1 mA = 0.001 A.

callouts.p: The rate of flow of electric charge.

core.h: What carries the charge in metals
core.p: In a metal wire the charge is carried by **free electrons** (delocalised electrons). These electrons are not tied to one atom, so they can drift through the metal when a potential difference is applied.
bullets: Electrons are **negatively charged**.
Metals are good conductors because they have many free electrons.
Insulators have very few free electrons, so almost no current can flow.
The electrons drift slowly, but they all start moving almost at once when the circuit is closed, so a lamp lights immediately.

callouts.p: Current in a metal is a flow of free electrons.

core.p: Charge only flows if two conditions are met. There must be a **closed circuit** (a complete conducting loop) and there must be a **source of potential difference**, such as a cell, battery or power supply, to push the charge round.
bullets: A break anywhere in a series loop (open switch, broken wire, blown lamp) stops the current everywhere in that loop.
The cell provides the potential difference that drives the charge.
Without a potential difference the free electrons just move randomly and there is no overall flow.
A complete loop of conductor with no cell has no current.

callouts.p: If asked why no current flows, name the missing condition: the circuit is not complete, or there is no source of potential difference.

core.p: By convention, current is drawn flowing from the **positive terminal to the negative terminal** of the cell. This was decided before electrons were discovered. Electrons actually move the **opposite way**, from negative to positive.
bullets: Conventional current: **+ to -** around the outside circuit.
Electron flow: **- to +** around the outside circuit.
Circuit arrows and symbols such as diodes use conventional current.
Both describe the same current; they are just opposite ways of describing it.

head: Description
Direction outside the cell
What it describes
rows: Direction a positive charge would move
Actual movement of electrons in metals

callouts.p: Do not say current flows from negative to positive unless the question asks about electron flow.

core.h: The equation Q = I x t
core.p: Because current is charge per second, the total charge that flows is current multiplied by time.
bullets: **charge (C) = current (A) x time (s)**, written Q = I t.
Rearranged: I = Q / t and t = Q / I.
Time must be in **seconds** before you substitute.
Current must be in **amps**: convert mA by dividing by 1000.

callouts.p: charge flow = current x time, Q = I t

core.p: Most mistakes in Q = I t questions come from units. Convert to amps and seconds first, then calculate.
bullets: minutes to seconds: multiply by 60.
hours to seconds: multiply by 3600.
mA to A: divide by 1000.
kC to C: multiply by 1000.
Give the answer in coulombs unless told otherwise.

callouts.p: Using 2 for 2 minutes instead of 120 s gives an answer 60 times too small.

core.p: In a single closed loop the current is the **same at every point**. Charge is not used up by components; the same charge that leaves the cell returns to it. What components use is energy, not charge.
bullets: Ammeters placed anywhere in a single loop give the same reading.
Charge is conserved: it is not used up.
Energy is transferred from the charge to components such as lamps.
This is why the rate of flow, Q per second, is the same everywhere in the loop.

callouts.p: Current is not used up by a lamp. The current before and after a lamp in a series loop is the same.

core.p: Current is measured with an **ammeter** connected **in series** with the component, so that all the charge flowing through the component also flows through the ammeter.
bullets: Break the circuit and insert the ammeter in the gap.
An ammeter has a very low resistance so it hardly affects the current.
Check the meter reads zero before switching on.
Choose a suitable range (A or mA) for the best resolution.

callouts.p: Ammeter in series, voltmeter in parallel. Examiners reward the exact word series.

core.p: If the current is constant, the charge that has flowed increases steadily with time. A graph of **charge Q against time t** is a straight line through the origin, and its **gradient equals the current**.
bullets: Gradient = change in Q / change in t = I.
A steeper line means a larger current.
A horizontal line means no further charge is flowing, so the current is zero.
If the current is doubled, twice as much charge flows in the same time.

core.h: Linking charge, current and time in reasoning
core.p: Many questions ask you to reason without numbers. Use the proportional relationships in Q = I t.
bullets: For a fixed time, charge is **directly proportional** to current.
For a fixed current, charge is **directly proportional** to time.
For a fixed charge, current and time are **inversely proportional**: twice the current delivers the charge in half the time.
A battery that can deliver a certain charge runs out faster when the current is larger.

callouts.p: Show the equation, substitution and answer with unit on separate lines to collect every method mark.

analogy.p: Think of a closed loop of pipe full of water with a pump. The water is the charge, the pump is the cell, and the current is how many litres pass a point each second. Because the pipe is a closed loop, the same flow passes every point and no water is used up, just as charge is not used up. The analogy breaks down because water pipes can leak or carry water without a full loop, whereas electric current needs a complete circuit, and the water's flow direction matches what moves, unlike conventional current which is opposite to electron flow.

terms.d: The rate of flow of electric charge.
A property of particles such as electrons; measured in coulombs (C).
The unit of charge; the charge passing a point when 1 A flows for 1 s.
The unit of current; 1 A is a flow of 1 coulomb per second.
One thousandth of an amp: 1 mA = 0.001 A.
Electrons in a metal that are not bound to one atom and can drift to carry current.
A complete loop of conductor that allows charge to flow.
The push from a source such as a cell that makes charge flow round a circuit.
Current drawn flowing from the positive terminal to the negative terminal.
The actual movement of electrons, from the negative terminal to the positive terminal.
A meter connected in series that measures current.
Connected one after another in a single loop, so the same current passes through each.
A material with many free charge carriers so current flows easily.
A material with very few free charge carriers so almost no current flows.

mistakes.w: Current is the flow of electrons from positive to negative.
mistakes.r: Current is the rate of flow of charge; conventional current is + to -, electrons flow - to +.

mistakes.w: Current is the amount of charge.
mistakes.r: Current is the rate of flow of charge: charge passing a point per second.

mistakes.w: Q = 0.5 x 3 = 1.5 C for 0.5 A for 3 minutes.
mistakes.r: Convert time to seconds: Q = 0.5 x 180 = 90 C.

mistakes.w: Current gets used up by the lamp so it is smaller after the lamp.
mistakes.r: Current is the same at every point in a series loop; energy, not charge, is transferred.

mistakes.w: Used 250 mA as 250 A in the equation.
mistakes.r: Convert mA to A by dividing by 1000: 250 mA = 0.25 A.

mistakes.w: Charge flows whenever there is a wire connected to a cell.
mistakes.r: Charge flows only when there is a closed circuit and a source of potential difference.

mistakes.w: The ammeter is connected in parallel with the lamp.
mistakes.r: The ammeter must be connected in series with the component.

mistakes.w: Gave the unit of charge as amps or A s only with no unit.
mistakes.r: Charge is measured in coulombs, C.

exam.q: Define electric current.
model: The rate of flow of (electric) charge.
exam.tip: The word rate is essential.

exam.q: State the unit of charge.
model: Coulomb (C).
exam.tip: Write the name or symbol clearly.

exam.q: State two conditions needed for a current to flow.
model: A closed (complete) circuit.
A source of potential difference, such as a cell.
exam.tip: Two separate points for two marks.

exam.q: A current of 2.0 A flows for 30 s. Calculate the charge that flows.
model: Q = 60 C
exam.tip: Include the unit.

exam.q: A charge of 360 C flows through a heater in 2 minutes. Calculate the current.
exam.tip: Convert minutes to seconds first.

exam.q: A torch bulb takes a current of 250 mA. Calculate how long it takes for 45 C of charge to flow through it.
exam.tip: Convert mA to A before dividing.

exam.q: Explain why the ammeter readings either side of a lamp in a series circuit are the same.
model: Charge is not used up by the lamp (it is conserved).
The same amount of charge passes each point per second, so the current is the same.
exam.tip: Say energy is transferred, not charge.

exam.q: Describe the difference between conventional current and electron flow.
model: Conventional current flows from positive to negative.
Electrons flow from negative to positive (opposite direction).
exam.tip: Give both directions.

exam.q: A phone battery delivers 0.40 A for 2.5 hours. Calculate the total charge delivered in kilocoulombs.
model: Q = 3.6 kC
exam.tip: 1 hour = 3600 s and 1 kC = 1000 C.

exam.q: Explain what is meant by a current of 1 ampere, and describe what happens to the charge passing a point if the current is doubled but the time stays the same.
model: 1 A is a flow of 1 coulomb of charge per second.
Q = I t, so charge is proportional to current for a fixed time.
Doubling the current doubles the charge that passes.
Twice as many electrons pass the point each second.
exam.tip: Use the equation to justify the proportion.

worked.q: A kettle draws a current of 12 A for 3 minutes. Calculate the charge that flows through it.
steps: Write the equation: Q = I t.
Convert time: 3 minutes = 3 x 60 = 180 s.
Substitute: Q = 12 x 180.
Calculate: Q = 2160 C.

worked.q: An LED has 1.8 C of charge flowing through it in 90 s. Calculate the current in mA.
steps: Rearrange: I = Q / t.
Substitute: I = 1.8 / 90.
Calculate: I = 0.020 A.
Convert to mA: 0.020 x 1000 = 20 mA.

worked.q: A battery can deliver 7200 C of charge. How long will it last, in hours, if the current is 0.50 A?
steps: Rearrange: t = Q / I.
Substitute: t = 7200 / 0.50.
Calculate: t = 14400 s.
Convert: 14400 / 3600 = 4.0 hours.
